extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and undergraduate linear algebra instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and assess undergraduate students' conceptions and difficulties about spanning sets, span (generated subspace), linear combinations, and vector representations; design interview tasks and interpret observable behaviors using APOS/semiotic frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object conception of solution set
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should demonstrate an object conception of this concept if they can represent in parametrical form the solution set of a given system or describe its geometric representation accurately. (Trigueros et al., 2007)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observable evidence: the student gives a parametric description of the solution set or an accurate geometric account; implies seeing the solution set as a mathematical object rather than only an algorithmic outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable understood as mathematical object
rubrics_metrics.description: Students need to work with variables as mathematical objects and understand variables as unknowns, general numbers, or parameters, and variables in functional relationships, and move flexibly between all these representations. (Trigueros and Ursini, 2003)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect students to shift roles of variables depending on context (e.g., treat some as parameters when forming parametric descriptions); confusion about variable roles indicates incomplete conceptualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action/process conception of linear combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Given V, S ⊂ V and a scalar field K, students must perform actions on vectors of S and scalars: perform scalar products and sums of vectors to obtain a new vector of V; coordination of these actions is interiorized into the process of construction of a new vector (linear combination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for students carrying out the component operations (scalar multiplication and vector addition) and reasoning about the procedural steps that produce linear combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process of finding scalars (solving system) as coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Through actions on S students verify if there are scalars in K to express elements of T as linear combinations of S; this is coordinated with the process of finding the solution set of the resulting system of equations (notion of variable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should include whether students link forming linear combinations to solving linear systems to find coefficients, i.e., they treat coefficient-finding as a process tied to variable interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encapsulation into spanning set object (object conception of spanning set)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the set S can be considered as a whole, this process has been encapsulated into an object called spanning set; students with an object conception can apply actions on the spanning set or the spanned set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: student reasons about the spanning set as a whole entity (manipulates sets, reasons about properties of spanning sets) rather than only executing elementwise procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-conception implications: non-uniqueness and element-count misconception
rubrics_metrics.description: The object conception implies students are able to explain that a given vector space can be generated by different spanning sets, that these sets do not necessarily have the same number of elements or common elements, and that the number of elements is not the only determining factor if a set is a spanning set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether students avoid the trap 'more vectors = larger span' and can articulate non-uniqueness of spanning sets and irrelevance of raw count without independence/dimension considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action conception of spanning set (observable behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students have an Action conception of spanning set and spanned set if they show a process conception of linear combination and can use it to verify if there are elements of K that can be used to write a specific vector from V as a linear combination of the vectors of S; when verifying span they may do it only with specific vectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: student tests spanning by checking a few particular vectors rather than a general argument; this indicates process/action level reasoning rather than generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process conception of spanning sets (generalization behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the student generalizes previous actions and mentally runs through elements of S to consider that every vector of V can be expressed as a linear combination of S, they display a process conception of spanning sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect general arguments (e.g., parameter counting, general solution forms) that show student has moved beyond case-based checks to a process that covers all vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination of two processes: belonging and linear combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: To find a spanning set of a given vector space, coordination of two underlying processes is necessary: (1) belonging to a set and (2) forming linear combinations; students tend to ignore the belonging part when working on spanning set tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks and scoring to detect whether students check that candidate spanning vectors actually belong to the subspace, not just that combinations produce desired vectors. Lack of coordination is a common obstacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between generating a subspace and constructing a spanning set
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a conceptual distinction (and possibly separate evolving conceptions) between generating a subspace from given vectors and, conversely, given a subspace finding a possible set of spanning vectors; students may not connect the constructions for the two tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment instruments should separate and probe both tasks: (a) given vectors, describe the generated subspace; (b) given a subspace, construct a spanning set — these can reveal different levels of understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of interview/task items for spanning concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview design should include questions whether a certain set spans a given vector space, construction-type questions (given a vector space, identify possible spanning sets), and comparisons of vector spaces generated by different spanning sets to shed light on difficulties and mental constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: include both verification and construction prompts, ask for justification and comparisons between different spanning sets; record and analyze verbal and written work to identify process/object conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belonging-of-vectors criterion (explicit assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly emphasize and assess the belonging of the vectors of a spanning set to the subspace they are claimed to span (e.g., question (5) in the study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring note: students who do not check membership of candidate spanning vectors to the subspace may produce incorrect justifications; include direct prompts that require membership checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-conception links to related concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Students who have a process conception of spanning sets can relate it to other concepts such as linear independence/dependence and dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for answers that connect spanning arguments to independence tests and dimensional reasoning; absence of such links indicates less-developed conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing spanning set is generally harder than deciding span
rubrics_metrics.description: It is easier for students to decide whether a given set spans a given vector space than to construct a spanning set for a given vector space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this empirical tendency to structure instruction and assessment: provide scaffolded construction tasks and expect lower performance relative to verification tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representations of vectors have a hierarchy and are context-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Vector representations have a strong hierarchy and are strongly dependent on the contexts of given questions; one cannot fully exploit multiple representations until understanding sufficient sophistication levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing vector understanding, consider which representations are appropriate for the context (geometric, symbolic, analytic, synthetic) and whether students can apply the correct level of representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semiotic representation components for translation tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformations between representations should be considered with three components of semiotic representation system: representation content, semiotic register used, and represented object. (Duval, 2006)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess translation ability by probing all three components: what the representation conveys, which register (graph, symbol, verbal) is used, and what mathematical object is being represented; failures may occur in any component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encapsulation/reification stages (operational→structural development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental stages (interiorization, condensation, reification) describe the move from operational (action/process) to structural/object conceptions; one should not expect structural conception without prior operational understanding. (Sfard, Dubinsky)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tasks that elicit procedural fluency first, then probe for reified/object-level reasoning; scoring should distinguish action-level answers from reified structural explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five key transitions for analyzing vector difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: Use five important transitions to frame analysis: (A) physics to mathematics, (B) arithmetic to algebraic, (C) analytic to synthetic, (D) geometric to symbolic, (E) concrete to abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assessment items that target each transition explicitly to diagnose where students struggle (e.g., physics→math: units vs. pure vectors; geometric→symbolic: diagram to algebraic form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ontological and epistemological axes to classify representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify vector representations along two axes: ontological (nature/existence of vectors: geometric vs symbolic, concrete vs abstract) and epistemological (ways of knowing: arithmetic→algebraic, analytic→synthetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework guidance: map tasks and student responses onto these axes to locate conceptual position and design targeted interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to translate among representation modes is critical
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' ability to understand mathematical concepts depends on their ability to make translations among several modes of representations (e.g., graph↔symbol↔verbal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should include explicit translation prompts; inability to translate indicates semiotic/instrumental obstacles rather than purely procedural gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research design criteria: identify difficulties and relative difficulty of representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Research questions should ask (1) what student difficulties in understanding and use of vector representations can be identified in undergraduate curricula, and (2) what generalizations about relative degree of difficulty of various representations are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing studies or rubrics, include instruments and analyses that can both catalogue error types and compare difficulty across representations and contexts.
